Read About Mecca

A trading town in a barren valley became the fixed point every Muslim on Earth turns toward five times a day — the story of how that happened runs through one building and one cave.

A shrine before Islam

The Kaaba predates Islam by an unknown span of centuries. Pre-Islamic Arabian tribes already treated the cube-shaped structure in the Meccan valley as a sanctuary, filling it with idols representing their various gods and making it the object of an annual pilgrimage. Mecca itself grew up around this shrine as a caravan-trading town, controlled by the Quraysh tribe, sitting on a route that connected Yemen to the Mediterranean. The Kaaba's black corner stone — venerated long before Muhammad's birth — was already being kissed and touched by pilgrims circling the structure.

The cave is barely large enough to sit in. What happened inside it is why every stop on this guide's second day exists.

The first revelation

Muhammad, born in Mecca around 570 CE, is said to have retreated regularly to a cave near the summit of Jabal al-Nour to meditate, away from the city's commerce and idol worship. Islamic tradition holds that it was in this cave, around 610 CE, that he received the first verses of what would become the Quran. The revelation continued over the following decades, and Muhammad's preaching against the city's polytheism put him at odds with the Quraysh, who controlled — and profited from — the Kaaba's pilgrimage trade.

Flight and return

By 622 CE the opposition had turned dangerous enough that Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for Medina, a migration known as the Hijra that marks year one of the Islamic calendar. Tradition holds that Muhammad and his companion Abu Bakr hid for three nights in a cave on Jabal Thawr, south of the city, while Quraysh search parties combed the surrounding hills, before slipping north to Medina by an indirect route. Eight years later, in 630 CE, Muhammad returned to Mecca at the head of a large following, took the city largely without bloodshed, and had the idols inside and around the Kaaba destroyed — rededicating the shrine to the worship of one God and setting the shape of the pilgrimage, Hajj, that continues today.

A mosque that keeps growing

Masjid al-Haram, the Grand Mosque built around the Kaaba, has been rebuilt and enlarged by nearly every major Islamic dynasty that followed — Umayyad, Abbasid, Ottoman, and, since the mid-20th century, the Saudi state, which has overseen the largest expansions in the mosque's history to accommodate a pilgrim population that has grown from the tens of thousands to millions each year. The Abraj Al-Bait complex and its Clock Tower, completed in 2012 directly across from the mosque, are the most visible sign of that growth — a modern skyline built specifically to house and feed the crowds the old city never had to.

One direction, five times a day

Whatever else has changed about Mecca — its population, its skyline, the nationality of the millions who pass through it each year — the Kaaba's role has not: it is the qibla, the fixed direction every Muslim faces in prayer, wherever in the world they happen to be standing. That single fact, more than any building or ritual, is what makes a barren trading valley the destination it is.
